```{r setup}
library(xchan)
library(sf)
```

This vignette covers creating channel objects from different data sources
and generating derived geometries.

There are two main objects in this package:

- A cross section (object of class `"xsection"`)
- A channel (object of class `"xchan"`)

A _cross section_ is a linear slice across a river channel, and in this
package, is spatially encoded through a _planimetric_ ("plan") view and,
optionally, a _profile_ view.

A _channel_ is a list of cross sections, optionally strung together along
a channel _axis_ like a centerline.

## Generating from spatial data


Since all channels are required to have planimetric cross sections, we start
with that, generating them from a bankline polygon. Here is a segment of the
Fraser River in British Columbia, Canada.

```{r}
plot(Squamish_bankline)
```

Cross sections can be auto-generated using the following algorithm. You can
specify the cross section spacing directly (`spacing`), or by the desired
number of cross sections (`n`).

```{r}
xt_generate_plan(Squamish_bankline, n = 100)
```

Channels are units-aware via the [**units**]() package if supplied (in this
case, through the bankline polygon's coordinate reference system (CRS)).
Raw numerics are interepreted in the base unit of the CRS. Here are cross
sections spaced 100 m apart.

```{r}
chan <- xt_generate_plan(Squamish_bankline, spacing = units::set_units(100, "m"))

# Plot
plot(Squamish_bankline, fill = "#7cb2fe")
plot(chan, add = TRUE)
```


```{r}
xt_axis(chan)
```



So far, this channel is only planimetric, with no profile view. If a profile view is important to you, you can get that from a DEM, piggybacking off the [**terra**]() package. The `xt_generate_profile()` adds a profile view to a pre-existing channel using a DEM, allowing you to sample the DEM by set spacing (`sample_freq`) or desired number of points (`sample_n`).

```{r}
Squamish_elev <- terra::unwrap(Squamish_dem)
chan <- xt_generate_profile(
  chan,
  dem = Squamish_elev,
  sample_freq = units::set_units(2, m)
)
```

While `plot()`ing a channel only ever shows the planimetric view, the profiles can be viewed by selecting individual cross sections.

```{r}
section <- xt_xsection_at(chan, 20)
section
plot(section, view = "profile")
```

## Creating Channels from Different Inputs

In other cases, it may be useful to experiment with hypothetical channels rather than requiring a real spatially surveyed channel. This is where the coercing tool `xt_as_channel()` is useful.

```{r}
widths <- c(2, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2)
plot(xt_as_channel(widths))
```

You can string these along a channel axis as well (interpreted here as a centerline):

```{r}
mat <- matrix(c(1:10, sin(1:10)), ncol = 2)
axis <- sf::st_linestring(mat, dim = "XY")
plot(axis)
plot(xt_as_channel(widths, axis = axis), add = TRUE)
```

Otherwise, you can specify cross sections from line segments from the [**sf**]() package.

```{r sfc-input}
# Create planimetric cross-sections
library(sf)

# Create simple line geometries
lines <- list(
  st_linestring(matrix(c(-2, -1, 5, 0), ncol = 2)),
  st_linestring(matrix(c(1, 0, 5, 0), ncol = 2)),
  st_linestring(matrix(c(3, 2, 3, -1), ncol = 2)),
  st_linestring(matrix(c(5, 4, -1, -2), ncol = 2))
)
plan_sfc <- st_sfc(lines)

# Create channel from sfc
channel <- xt_as_channel(plan_sfc)
plot(channel)
```

## Combining a channel with tabular data

Channel objects are deliberately plan lists, so that you can control each cross section. It is also useful to store additional information about cross sections alongside them, like the grain size or bed roughness coefficient. Because channels are just lists, they can go in a list-column in a data frame. There is no special **xchan** structure here; it's possible it will be native in a future version of the package, but at this stage, just use your favourite workflow for this.

```{r df-input}
chan_tbl <- tibble::tibble(channel = channel, roughness = 0.035)
chan_tbl
```



## Channel axis and ordering

Channels have a stored _axis_ whose main purpose is to define a cross section ordering. strings cross sections together in order. 

In this case, since it was not supplied, `xt_generate_plan()` auto-generated the axis using the centerline of the provided bankline polygon (from the [**centerline**]() package). This axis is also used by `xt_generate_plan()` to sample equally spaced cross sections.

It's important to note that ordering of the cross sections in the channel list is not necessarily in flow order (more on why later). You can rearrange or even subset cross sections while the flow order is still preserved.

```{r}
chan2 <- chan[c(4, 2, 3, 1)]
```

If you ever find your cross sections listed out-of-order, you can arrange it like so:

```{r}
xt_arrange_downstream(channel)
```

You can get and set the axis.

```{r channel-axis}
# Trace an axis along the channel from cross-section midpoints
centerline <- xt_trace_centerline(channel)
plot(channel)
plot(centerline, add = TRUE, col = "red", lwd = 2)
```

For flexible modelling, there's a function that allows you to change the flow direction.

```{r}
xt_reverse_flow(channel)
```



## Spatial Outputs

Converting to `sfc`

```{r sfc-outputs}
plan_sfc <- xt_as_sfc(channel, what = "plan")
# profile_sfc <- xt_as_sfc(channel, what = "profile")

st_length(plan_sfc)
```

To combine with non-spatial columns in an `sf` object, use for example
`sf::st_sf(your_df, geometry = xt_as_sfc(channel, what = "plan"), crs = st_crs(plan_sfc))`.
